title.en: History: The World after World War II

text.en: Raju heard of a long rivalry between two big powers without a direct war. "The Cold War," said the teacher.

After World War II the United Nations was formed in 1945 to keep peace. Two superpowers, the USA (capitalist) and the USSR (communist), began a rivalry called the Cold War, which did not involve direct fighting between them.
The world split into blocs with NATO led by the USA and the Warsaw Pact led by the USSR. India and other countries followed the Non-Aligned Movement, staying out of both blocs.
Colonies in Asia and Africa gained independence, and the Cold War ended when the USSR broke up in 1991. The Korean and Vietnam wars and the Cuban Missile Crisis were key events.
After World War II the United Nations was formed in 1945 to keep peace.
Two superpowers, the USA (capitalist) and the USSR (communist), began a rivalry called the Cold War, which did not involve direct fighting between them.
The world split into blocs with NATO led by the USA and the Warsaw Pact led by the USSR.
India and other countries followed the Non-Aligned Movement, staying out of both blocs.
Colonies in Asia and Africa gained independence, and the Cold War ended when the USSR broke up in 1991.
The Korean and Vietnam wars and the Cuban Missile Crisis were key events.
After 1945, war-ruined Britain and France stepped back from superpower status, leaving a bipolar world dominated by the United States and the Soviet Union.
In Europe, Soviet-backed communist governments took root in eastern states—an ideological divide Winston Churchill famously called the 'Iron Curtain'.

board.text: Iron Curtain divides East & West Europe

text.en: Under the 1947 Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan, the USA poured billions of dollars into rebuilding Western Europe so communism would not spread there.

board.text: Truman Doctrine & Marshall Plan aid Europe

text.en: In 1949 the USA and Western allies formed NATO for collective defence, and in 1955 the USSR answered with the Warsaw Pact.
Germany split into capitalist West Germany and communist East Germany, with the concrete Berlin Wall standing from 1961 to 1989 as a stark symbol of division.
Meanwhile in Asia, Mao Zedong led the Chinese Communist Party to victory in 1949, establishing the People's Republic of China.
Cold War tension flared into proxy wars in Korea (1950–1953), leaving Korea divided along the 38th Parallel, and later in the long Vietnam War.
In 1962, the Cuban Missile Crisis pushed humanity to the brink of nuclear war for thirteen tense days before President Kennedy and Nikita Khrushchev compromised.
Refusing to become pawns in either bloc, newly freed Asian and African countries—inspired by Bandung 1955—built the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) in 1961.
Under Nehru, Nasser, Tito, Sukarno and Nkrumah, NAM fought colonialism, nuclear brinkmanship and apartheid across continents.
Look at West Asia too: Israel's creation in 1948 sparked recurring Arab–Israeli conflicts and Palestinian displacement that continue to affect world diplomacy.
Across the 1950s and 1960s, a wave of decolonisation swept Asia and Africa—after India (1947), Indonesia, Ghana, Algeria and Kenya won independence.
In South Africa, Nelson Mandela led the long struggle against racist apartheid until multiracial democracy finally dawned in 1994.
From 1948, European rivals chose cooperation instead of war—gradually building the European Economic Community and today's European Union (Maastricht Treaty, 1992).

board.text: European unity grows into the EU

text.en: Notice another landmark: in 1948 the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), championed by leaders like Eleanor Roosevelt and Hansa Mehta.

board.text: 1948: UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights

text.en: By the 1980s, Soviet factories stagnated under heavy military spending and rigid planning, leading reformist leader Mikhail Gorbachev to introduce Glasnost and Perestroika.
Glasnost meant political openness and free speech; Perestroika sought economic restructuring—unleashing peaceful democratic movements across Eastern Europe.
On 9 November 1989, joyous crowds tore down the Berlin Wall, uniting East and West Germany the following year.

board.text: Nov 1989: Fall of the Berlin Wall

text.en: On 25 December 1991, the Soviet Union dissolved into fifteen independent republics, ending the forty-five-year Cold War.

board.text: Dec 1991: Dissolution of USSR ends Cold War

text.en: Yet the post-1991 era quickly saw globalisation, rising Asian economies like India and China, digital revolutions and climate challenges.
Check the twin lessons cleanly: nuclear arms races waste wealth and endanger everyone, while peaceful openness dismantled walls.
Remember key milestones: 1945 UN -> 1949 China & NATO -> 1961 NAM -> 1962 Cuba -> 1989 Berlin Wall -> 1991 USSR ends.
To trace the big causal arc: WWII vacuum -> bipolar Cold War + NAM third way -> Soviet crisis & Gorbachev -> unified multipolar world.

board.text: Bipolar rivalry -> Reform -> Cold War ends

text.en: Understanding the post-WWII world explains today's United Nations, European Union, NAM heritage and independent Asian and African nations.

problem.en: How did Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms unintentionally speed up the end of the Cold War between 1985 and 1991?

text.en: Notice the Soviet crisis.

why.en: Decades of arms racing with the USA left Soviet consumer goods scarce and Eastern European allies restless.

text.en: See how Glasnost & Perestroika worked.

why.en: Gorbachev allowed political debate (Glasnost), tried market flexibility (Perestroika) and refused to use Soviet tanks to crush Eastern European protests.

text.en: Trace the result.

why.en: Once citizens could speak freely without fear of troops, the Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and Soviet republics became independent in 1991.

prompt.en: A friend says The Cold War was a direct war between the USA and USSR. How will you reply?
